title: How Does I'm Not a Robot Know You're Human?
sources: Wikipedia 'CAPTCHA' and IBM 'What is CAPTCHA?' (ibm.com/think/topics/captcha): CAPTCHA = Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart, a challenge easy for humans but hard for bots, used to stop spam sign-ups, ticket scalping bots and similar abuse; coined in 2003 at Carnegie Mellon

Google Security Blog, 'Are you a robot? Introducing No CAPTCHA reCAPTCHA' (Dec 2014) and Radware 'reCAPTCHA: How it works': the checkbox runs an advanced risk analysis of the user's whole engagement (mouse movement, timing, browser and cookie signals) before, during and after the click; suspicious users get an image challenge

Wikipedia 'reCAPTCHA' and The Register 'Google acquires reCAPTCHA' (Sept 2009): the distorted words came from scanned books and New York Times archives, so solving them helped digitize text for Google Books
TechCrunch, 'Google Now Using ReCAPTCHA To Decode Street View Addresses' (29 March 2012): reCAPTCHA showed house numbers from Street View images to help Google Maps read addresses

lines.text: How does the I'm not a robot box know you're human?
lines.caps: HOW *DOES | THE I'M *NOT | A *ROBOT BOX | KNOW YOU'RE *HUMAN?

lines.text: It's a Captcha, a test that's easy for people
so bots can't spam sign-ups or grab every concert ticket.
lines.caps: SO BOTS *CAN'T | *SPAM SIGN-UPS | OR *GRAB | EVERY CONCERT *TICKET

lines.text: But the checkbox isn't really the test.
Before you even click, it watches how your mouse moves,
and checks your browser and cookies.
Real people wobble and pause, but simple bots move too perfectly.
lines.caps: REAL PEOPLE *WOBBLE | AND *PAUSE | BUT SIMPLE *BOTS | MOVE TOO *PERFECTLY

lines.text: Look suspicious, and you get the picture puzzle instead.
those squiggly words you typed years ago helped scan old books,
and those house numbers helped Google read Street View.
So proving you're human might mean doing free work.
